title: Red Oil Wontons
subtitle: Sichuan-style wontons dressed in chilli oil, sesame sauce, and vinegar
excerpt: Plump pork-and-ginger wontons are boiled then napped with a Sichuan dressing of chilli oil, sesame paste, and black vinegar. The dressing takes two minutes; the folding takes a bit longer. Makes 24 wontons in about 45 minutes.
sourceNotes: Hong you chao shou (red oil wontons) is a staple of Chengdu street food and appears in Fuchsia Dunlop's Sichuan Cookery as one of the defining small dishes (xiao chi) of the province. The term chao shou (crossed arms) refers to the folded shape of the Sichuan wonton, which differs from Cantonese versions in its crossing of the two far corners. The chilli oil dressing tradition is part of a broader category of Sichuan cold sauces that balance ma (numbing), la (hot), suan (sour), and xian (savoury).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked wontons in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a bag. Cook from frozen in boiling water, adding 2 extra minutes to the cooking time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Filled wontons can be covered and refrigerated for up to 4 hours before cooking.

content.text: This makes 24 wontons and takes about 45 minutes. The filling is simple -- pork mince, ginger, spring onion, and a little soy -- and the
wonton wrappers
are shop-bought. The dressing is where the work is: good
chilli oil
with sediment, Chinkiang black vinegar, and
sesame paste
make the difference between a dressed wonton and a good one.

Do not overfill the wontons -- a heaped teaspoon of filling is enough. The wrapper needs to seal cleanly with no air pockets, which are the main cause of splitting in the water. Keep a bowl of cold water nearby to wet the edges before sealing.
What you need
Method

Combine all filling ingredients in a bowl and mix in one direction for 2 minutes until the mixture develops a slightly sticky, cohesive texture. This builds the protein structure that holds the filling together during cooking. Refrigerate for 10 minutes.

Make the dressing. Whisk together the chilli oil, sesame paste thinned with water, vinegar, soy sauce, sugar, garlic, and ground Sichuan peppercorns. Taste -- it should be sharp, nutty, spicy, and gently sweet. Set aside.

Set up a filling station: wonton wrappers, filling, a small bowl of cold water, and a tray lined with baking paper. Place a wrapper on a clean surface. Add a heaped teaspoon of filling just below centre.

Wet the edges of the wrapper lightly with water. Fold the wrapper over the filling to form a triangle, pressing firmly to expel all air pockets and seal the edges. Then pick up the triangle with the filling end pointing away from you. Wet one of the far corners and bring both corners around to meet at the front, pressing to seal. The wonton should look like a nurses cap. Place on the lined tray. Repeat with the remaining wrappers and filling.
Bring a large saucepan of water to a rolling boil. Add the wontons in batches of 8-10. When they float to the surface, cook for a further 2 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain briefly.
Spoon the dressing into serving bowls. Add the wontons and toss gently to coat. Finish with extra ground
Sichuan peppercorns
and sliced spring onions. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Air pocket trapped inside the seal, or wrappers were too dry to adhere
items.fix: Press firmly around the filling to push out any air before sealing. Wet the edges generously -- the moisture activates the starch in the wrapper and acts as glue.

items.cause: Pork was over-mixed or cooked at too high a temperature
items.fix: Mix the filling just enough to bring it together. Simmer the wontons gently; a hard rolling boil can make the filling tough.

items.cause: Sesame paste was not thinned, blocking the other flavours, or the vinegar was omitted
items.fix: Thin the sesame paste to a pourable consistency before adding. The vinegar sharpness is essential -- add more if the dressing tastes heavy or one-dimensional.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Red oil wontons are a Sichuan snack and starter. They are sold at street stalls and served at dim sum. The sauce is the point: a balance of chilli oil heat, sesame depth, vinegar brightness, and soy salinity. Make extra sauce and keep it in the fridge for up to a week.
